bottom_line: In patients with early atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular conditions, early rhythm control vs usual care reduced the first primary composite outcome (hazard ratio, 0.79; 96% confidence interval, 0.66 to 0.94).
implications: These data support that, in this population, early rhythm control was associated with a lower rate of the composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalization with worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome (3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio, 0.79; 96% CI, 0.66 to 0.94) without a significant difference in annual nights spent in hospital (5.8±21.9 vs 5.1±15.5 days per year; P = 0.23). They also support that overall primary composite safety events were similar (16.6% vs 16.0%), while serious adverse events of special interest related to rhythm-control therapy were more frequent with early rhythm control (4.9% vs 1.4%).

major_points.text: International, parallel-group, randomized, open, blinded-outcome-assessment trial in early atrial fibrillation diagnosed within 1 year.
major_points.quote: In this international, investigator-initiated, parallel-group, randomized, open, blinded-outcome- assessment trial, we randomly assigned patients who had early atrial fibrillation (diagnosed ≤1 year before enrollment)

major_points.text: Trial population: 2789 patients randomized across 135 centers with median 36 days since AF diagnosis.
major_points.quote: In 135 centers, 2789 patients with early atrial fibrillation (median time since di- agnosis, 36 days) underwent randomization.

major_points.text: First primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalization for worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome.
major_points.quote: The first primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, stroke, or hospitalization with worsening of heart failure or acute coronary syn- drome

major_points.text: First primary outcome occurred less often with early rhythm control than usual care.
major_points.quote: A first-primary-outcome event occurred in 249 of the patients assigned to early rhythm control (3.9 per 100 person-years) and in 316 patients assigned to usual care (5.0 per 100 person-years) (hazard ratio, 0.79; 96% confidence interval, 0.66 to 0.94; P = 0.005).

major_points.text: Second primary outcome (nights in hospital per year) did not differ significantly between groups.
major_points.quote: The mean (±SD) number of nights spent in the hospital did not differ significantly between the groups (5.8±21.9 and 5.1±15.5 days per year, respectively; P = 0.23).

major_points.text: Primary composite safety outcome did not differ; rhythm-control-therapy serious adverse events were more frequent in early rhythm control.
major_points.quote: The percentage of patients with a primary safety outcome event did not differ signifi- cantly between the groups; serious adverse events related to rhythm-control ther- apy occurred in 4.9% of the patients assigned to early rhythm control and 1.4% of the patients assigned to usual care.

major_points.text: At 2 years, sinus rhythm was more frequent with early rhythm control than usual care.
major_points.quote: Sinus rhythm was found more often in pa- tients who had been randomly assigned to receive early rhythm control (84.9% at 1 year, 82.1% at 2 years) than in patients assigned to receive usual care (65.5% at 1 year, 60.5% at 2 years)

major_points.text: Trial stopped early for efficacy at the third interim analysis after median 5.1 years follow-up per patient.
major_points.quote: The trial was stopped for efficacy at the third interim analysis after a median of 5.1 years of follow-up per patient.

criticisms.text: Open trial design was necessary; authors used blinded central assessment to minimize bias.
criticisms.quote: We compared two treatment strategies that ne- cessitated an open trial design. Blinded, central assessment of primary outcomes was used to minimize bias.

criticisms.text: Not primarily designed to assess safety/effectiveness of specific components of early rhythm control.
criticisms.quote: The trial was not primarily de- signed to assess the safety and effectiveness of specific components of early rhythm control.

criticisms.text: Generalizability may be limited to early AF; results may not apply when rhythm-control (including ablation) is initiated later.
criticisms.quote: We enrolled only patients with early atrial fibrilla- tion, and thus the results may not be generaliz- able to patients in whom rhythm-control therapy that includes atrial fibrillation ablation is initi- ated later.

criticisms.text: Further analysis needed on costs of early rhythm control.
criticisms.quote: Further analysis is needed of the costs of early rhythm control.

criticisms.text: Eligibility for either strategy may have excluded the most symptomatic patients.
criticisms.quote: All enrolled patients were deemed eligible for either rate-control or rhythm- control therapy, which probably excluded the most symptomatic patients.

criticisms.text: No detailed information collected on recurrent AF in both groups; sinus rhythm percentages not comparable to recurrent AF data from other trials.
criticisms.quote: We did not collect detailed information on recurrent atrial fibrillation in both groups, and therefore our data on percent- ages of patients with sinus rhythm are not com- parable to data on recurrent atrial fibrillation
